# Open Knowledge Models

Not open-weight models. Something better.

Politicians, journalists, VCs, and tech CEOs are arguing about open versus closed models and what they mean for humanity's future. In light of the Jensen story, we should consider that neither may be the right answer for keeping humans in control.

We propose Open Knowledge Models — not open-weight models — as the solution.

Open Knowledge Models > Open-Weight Models > Closed Models

## What is this jargon?

Closed models are primarily what comes out of Anthropic and OpenAI. All we know about them is the documentation the companies publish. We don't know whether it's one model or many models working in a loop or graph internally.

Open-weight models are relatively easy to understand. You can download them and run them on your own hardware. Qwen3.8-27B and Inkling-2 are two examples.

Both types of models consume a copy of the internet, including copyrighted works that were pirated, distilled, and mixed into the weights — where they bear little resemblance to the original human work they were derived from.

There is now a conflict between model companies over which types of distillation are permissible and which ones constitute an "attack."

These are small models in the 1–10B parameter range that hold minimal information in their weights. The majority of their knowledge lives in an external database. The idea is to maintain a cognitive core and an external knowledge base.

This idea was popularized by Andrej Karpathy in a 2024 podcast , but it has been gathering dust in mainstream American academic research and industry work. Chinese and German academics, however, continue to pursue it.

## What are the benefits?

Unlike the current generation of models, which melds cognition and knowledge into the weights and obscures the difference between public, copyrighted, proprietary, and private data, it is possible to maintain separate databases in the same latent space.

This would solve many of the problems that Alex Karp, the CEO of Palantir, brings up.

## Are these ideas anti-capitalist?

No. We think they're a great way to promote commerce in proprietary, domain-specific datasets and to ensure that AI remains explainable and understandable by humans.

The principle is simple: we can't control what we don't understand.

## Are they limited to data?

No — the same ideas apply to code. Instead of having AI write a million lines of code and two million lines of proof, it makes sense to build a software pipeline that starts at a high level of abstraction and gradually lowers it. We call it the diffusion model of programming .

A small number of human experts will be proficient at each stage of the pipeline and can monitor what the AI is doing.

Principle: a human should be able to understand if and why the AI messed up — and be able to train fellow practitioners so the knowledge can be passed on.

## What should we do?

Call your congressman or senator and tell them the government should invest in Open Knowledge Models and transpiler-based coding pipelines.

If Americans don't do it, other countries will.
